title: Robotic welding automation
role: Graduate Research Assistant · Advisor: Dr. Prabhakar Pagilla
summary: A UR10e and Miller pulsed-MIG welding platform that connects workpiece registration, weld-path planning, and coordinated robot execution through a Python/ROS interface.
challenge: Automating a weld requires more than moving a torch between two points. The CAD model has to agree with the physical workpiece, the torch has to maintain its orientation and travel speed, and the welding equipment has to be triggered in step with the robot's motion.
contributions: Equipment and operator interface

Built a Python/PyQt5/ROS interface for weld setup and execution. Integrated Arduino PWM and relay control with the Miller welder for arc voltage, wire feed, and weld triggering, and brought registration and RViz into the operator workflow.
CAD-to-robot registration

Used three torch-probed reference points with Kabsch alignment and ICP refinement to establish the workpiece-to-robot transform. This connected CAD geometry to the physical setup without external metrology.
Path generation and robot motion

Generated weld paths from STL edges and surface normals with a 45° torch tilt. Developed the planning workflow around inverse kinematics, wrist-limit handling, and joint continuity. The GUI execution pipeline uses MoveIt planning, angle unwrapping, and distance-based trajectory timing to sequence approach, welding, retreat, and reorientation.
Execution and motion checks

Coordinated weld triggering with robot execution and added end-effector logging, joint-continuity checks, and checks for abrupt joint motion and jerk. The operator interface connects planned motion to the robot and welding equipment.
Closed-loop weld-pool regulation

Integrated Optris PI 05M infrared monitoring and used bead-height and calibrated temperature feedback for closed-loop regulation of torch travel speed and arc voltage. This connects the measured weld-pool state to the robot-motion and welding-parameter commands.
outcome: The project brought equipment control, CAD registration, trajectory generation, execution monitoring, and closed-loop weld-pool regulation into one workflow. The original report captures the system architecture and sensing setup; the closed-loop work was completed subsequently.

benchmark.text: The relevant comparison criteria are error relative to the desired weld geometry and thermal state, transient response when the reference or process conditions change, and agreement between in-process estimates and post-weld measurements. These criteria provide a framework for evaluating the closed loop; the references below are literature context, not numerical results from this system.

title: Robot motion and feedback control at MIKO
summary: Two years developing motion and control software for expressive articulation, self-balancing mobility, and audio-directed interaction on physical robots.
challenge: An interactive robot must turn sensing into motion that is stable, repeatable, and expressive. My work connected dynamic modeling and controller design to joint motion, balance, and directional responses on robot hardware.
contributions: Head-motion manipulator

Developed control and path-planning software for expressive joint-level articulation. Used system identification, stability testing, and robust controller synthesis to connect a model of the mechanism to its physical response.
Self-balancing mobility
Extended the control work to a self-balancing robot, integrating its sensor suite and tuning robust controllers to maintain balance.
Audio-directed motion

Connected direction-of-arrival estimates from audio processing to yaw-axis control so the robot could turn toward an active speaker. Also implemented remote-control functionality for the mobile platform.
outcome: This role gave me experience taking control algorithms through modeling, implementation, sensor integration, and hardware testing. It continues to shape how I approach robotic automation: understand the dynamics, make the feedback path explicit, and evaluate the behavior on the system.

title: LPV-MPC vehicle tracking
summary: A custom Python controller that schedules its prediction model with speed and curvature, tracks three driving routes, and enforces steering, acceleration, and command-rate limits.
challenge: A tracking controller must anticipate curves while respecting how far and how quickly its actuators can move. This project develops a new linear parameter-varying model predictive control (LPV-MPC) implementation and tests its recovery from an initial offset and an unmodeled disturbance.
contributions: Vehicle model and tracking coordinates

Developed a four-state nonlinear kinematic bicycle simulator with position, heading, and speed. Defined along-track, cross-track, heading, and speed errors in the moving reference frame. A separate RK4 integrator propagates the simulated vehicle.
Prediction model and optimization

Derived a local error model scheduled by reference speed and curvature across a 20-step horizon. At each 100 ms update, custom Python code assembles a sparse quadratic program balancing tracking error, feedforward commands, and command changes. OSQP solves the numerical optimization.
Actuator and speed constraints

Included ±25° steering, ±35°/s steering-rate, −2.5 to +2.0 m/s² acceleration, ±3.0 m/s³ commanded-jerk, and 1–10 m/s predicted-speed bounds. Each run separately checks the commands and sampled nonlinear vehicle speed against those limits.
Custom experiments and plots

Created analytic oval, figure-eight, and lane-change routes. Every run starts with the same tracking offset; the lane-change case also receives a lateral drift and longitudinal load from 24 to 26 seconds. The plots show trajectory tracking, error recovery, and actuator constraints.
outcome: All 1,520 optimization steps across the three scenarios returned a solved status, and the applied commands, command rates, and sampled speeds passed the configured limit checks within numerical tolerance. The table reports root mean square error (RMSE) over every recorded state, including startup recovery. These are results from the new custom simulation.
sourceNote: This implementation builds on the LPV-MPC concepts studied in my earlier Mark Misin–based project. The figures show results from the new custom simulation, using OSQP for numerical optimization.

benchmark.title: Model and evaluation scope
benchmark.text: The prediction model is a local LPV approximation around the reference trajectory. These experiments use a four-state kinematic vehicle, perfect state feedback, and a known reference; they do not model tire slip, measurement noise, or actuator lag. The 100 ms interval is a simulation setting. The new scenarios are separate from the earlier six-state reference-code study, so their errors are not a like-for-like performance comparison.

title: Perception and planning for rural roads
eyebrow: Autonomous Vehicles for All · Perception & planning
role: Graduate Research Assistant · Advisor: Dr. Reza Langari
summary: Frenet-frame trajectory planning and camera/LiDAR perception for marked and unmarked gravel roads, with evaluation under difficult visibility and sensor conditions.
imageAlt: Annotated AVA research vehicle with its sensor locations
imageCaption: AVA research vehicle and sensor layout, from the team's technical overview. My contribution focused on perception and motion planning.
challenge: Lane markings alone are not enough for rural-road driving. Unmarked gravel, glare, low light, and dust make road boundaries uncertain, while asynchronous camera, LiDAR, and odometry data complicate the planner's view of the environment.
contributions: Frenet-frame planning
Developed a motion planner that generated candidate trajectories using lateral offsets and velocity profiles. Selected feasible candidates using curvature constraints and a weighted cost function.
Perception and coordinate alignment

Tuned CLRerNet lane detection and SAM drivable-area segmentation to supply road-boundary estimates. Aligned camera, LiDAR, and odometry data in a shared map frame for the ROS perception and planning pipeline.
Evaluation under degraded inputs

Tested using ROS bags and simulation with low light, glare, dust, unmarked gravel, sensor dropout, and timing jitter. Adjusted perception thresholds and temporal smoothing to address degraded trajectory candidates and maintain lane continuity.
Visual-token analysis

Studied visual-token redundancy in OpenDriveVLA across 6,019 nuScenes validation samples. Approximately 10 principal components captured 80% of scene-token variance and 97% of map-token variance. This suggested opportunities for token reduction; variance retention alone does not establish a deployed inference speedup.
outcome: The work connected road perception to feasible trajectory selection and examined how the pipeline behaved when visibility or sensor timing degraded. Evaluation used recorded data and simulation; the vehicle photographs document the AVA research platform.

title: Semantic frontier exploration
role: Graduate Researcher · Advisor: Dr. Srikanth Saripalli
summary: Developing semantic value maps and viewpoint selection for robot exploration when geometric coverage leaves important areas hidden by clutter or occlusion.
challenge: A geometrically explored map can still leave a robot with poor views of important areas. Clutter, occlusion, and restricted viewpoints motivate exploration that considers the semantic value of another observation as well as travel cost.
contributions: Semantic value mapping
Developing a 2D map that projects image–text relevance scores using depth and robot pose, with visibility-based weighting to fuse observations.
Frontier and viewpoint selection
Formulating frontier ranking using semantic map values, expected information gain, and travel cost to guide further inspection.
Multi-robot evaluation framework

Building a ROS 2/Gazebo Husky–Jackal framework with LiDAR mapping, cameras, coordinate transforms, and extended Kalman filter localization to evaluate frontier selection under occlusion and limited viewpoint access.
outcome: This research is in progress. Evaluation will examine whether semantic and visibility information can guide useful inspection beyond geometric coverage.

title: Robust control for vehicle platooning
summary: Longitudinal and lateral control of a three-vehicle platoon, comparing PID and sliding-mode approaches through tracking error and control effort.
imageAlt: Master's thesis plot of lateral tracking error using super-twisting control
imageCaption: Lateral tracking error with super-twisting control, reproduced from my master's thesis.
challenge: A vehicle platoon must maintain spacing while following a reference path. The study examined the tradeoffs among convergence, overshoot, chattering, and control effort for nonlinear vehicle dynamics.
contributions: Dynamics and state estimation
Modeled three vehicles using nonlinear bicycle dynamics in MATLAB/Simulink, with a reference speed of 8 m/s. Used a Luenberger observer to estimate yaw rate from lateral velocity.
Controller comparison
Implemented PID, conventional sliding mode control, power-rate exponential reaching law (PREL), and super-twisting control for the longitudinal and lateral channels.
Quantitative evaluation
Compared integral tracking-error measures and control energy across the three vehicles. Examined both path-following behavior and maintenance of longitudinal spacing.
outcome: PREL produced the lowest reported error indices in the comparison. Super-twisting provided lateral convergence without overshoot and the lowest longitudinal control energy. These results highlight the tradeoff between tracking accuracy and control effort in the simulated platoon.

title: A robot swarm searching for light
summary: Particle swarm optimization on three LEGO NXT robots, using light measurements, overhead ArUco tracking, and obstacle sensing to locate the brightest spot.
imageAlt: LEGO NXT robot carrying an ArUco tracking marker
imageCaption: One of the robot platforms used in the bachelor's project, with an ArUco marker for overhead localization.
challenge: The brightest location is initially unknown, and each robot can only measure light at its current position. A shared search strategy needs localization, communication, navigation, and obstacle handling to work on real robots.
contributions: Search and coordination
Implemented particle swarm optimization to update robot destinations using personal-best and swarm-best light measurements. Used MATLAB for simulation and Python in the hardware workflow.
Localization and communication
Used an overhead camera and ArUco markers to estimate robot positions. Connected the camera to the central system over USB and the three NXT robots over Bluetooth.
Physical navigation

Integrated light and ultrasonic sensors with the robots. The central system issued destination coordinates, while obstacle handling allowed robots to change their paths around static obstacles and other robots.
outcome: The robots converged to the brightest region in the reported hardware trials. One documented successful trial used 11 iterations, with arrival times of 130, 188, and 264 seconds. The related ICECA 2019 paper received a Best Paper Award.

title: EKF-SLAM and embedded robot navigation
eyebrow: IIT Bombay internship · Estimation & embedded control
role: Summer intern · Joint project with Alden J. Joseph
summary: A study of joint robot-pose and landmark estimation in MATLAB, alongside ultrasonic obstacle avoidance and encoder-based navigation on a SPARK-V robot.
imageAlt: MATLAB EKF-SLAM simulation showing a robot path and landmark estimates
imageCaption: EKF-SLAM simulation from the internship report, showing a waypoint route and estimated landmarks.
challenge: A mobile robot must reason about its pose while its sensors and motion are noisy. This project combined a simulation study of probabilistic mapping with a separate physical implementation of obstacle-avoiding navigation.
contributions: SLAM simulation
Adapted a MATLAB EKF-SLAM simulator for joint pose and landmark estimation. Studied Jacobian linearization and nearest-neighbor data association with Mahalanobis gating.
Mapping behavior
Observed reduced landmark uncertainty over repeated waypoint traversals. Extended the simulator with reactive steering using three sensor views to navigate around landmarks without preset waypoints.
Embedded navigation

Implemented navigation on a SPARK-V robot in Embedded C for its ATmega16 controller. Combined ultrasonic obstacle avoidance with wheel-encoder distance feedback and demonstrated traversal of a room containing obstacles.
outcome: The work connected the mathematics of estimation to practical mobile-robot sensing and control. EKF-SLAM was studied in MATLAB; the SPARK-V demonstration implemented obstacle avoidance and encoder feedback rather than a full onboard SLAM stack.

title: Needle-tip tracking with Kalman filtering
summary: Combining ultrasound image processing and a four-state Kalman filter to estimate needle-tip position when speckle obscures the visual measurement.
challenge: Ultrasound speckle can make a needle tip difficult to detect consistently. I combined geometric image processing with state estimation to maintain a position estimate through uncertain visual observations.
contributions: Visual measurement
Built a LabVIEW pipeline using background subtraction, edge detection, and region-of-interest RANSAC line fitting to extract needle features.
State estimation
Used a four-state Kalman filter to combine measurements over time and maintain needle-tip position estimates when speckle obscured the tip.
Experimental comparison
Compared the estimates against an NDI-Aurora electromagnetic tracker in artificial and biological tissue, with insertion depths up to 6.5 cm.
outcome: Compared with vision-only tracking, position root mean square error (RMSE) decreased from 0.79 cm to 0.03 cm in artificial tissue and from 0.84 cm to 0.21 cm in biological tissue. These results apply to the artificial- and biological-tissue experimental setup.
sourceNote: Methods and reported RMSE values from my 2026 résumé.
